name: PT Rukun Raharja Tbk
industry_name: Gas & fuel distribution, refining and marketing

frontmatter.title: Rukun Raharja: a gas infrastructure build with a konglo price
frontmatter.summary: We initiate Rukun Raharja at HOLD with a target of Rp390 and a twelve-month total return of 3.1%. The twelve-month fundamental value is Rp313; the shares at Rp394 trade above it, and the konglo lens keeps part of the premium, lifting the target. The gas-infrastructure build is real, but half-year profit is flattered by non-recurring gains and the balance sheet is more levered than the fiscal-year accounts show.
thesis: Rukun Raharja is the largest private gas trader in Indonesia and is widening into midstream compression, pipelines and LNG infrastructure; the Sengkang compressor moved the group's gross margin to a new, higher plane in the first half of 2026.

The reported profit surge is only partly operating: bargain-purchase gains on the Madura participating interest, Hafar associate income and oil-linked Cepu income explain a material share of first-half earnings, and those fade as the oil deck normalises.

The DCF at Rp320 and the gas-peer EV/EBITDA cross-check at Rp202 do not cluster: the multiple is a low gas-downstream median applied to trailing EBITDA, and we weight the DCF at seventy per cent and the cross-check at thirty per cent.

The dividend-yield method is switched off on method fit: the current gas-peer median yield values RAJA well below the DCF, so removing it raises the blend by about three per cent rather than lowering it, but a dividend method cannot anchor a business whose payout is subordinate to a multi-year capex build; we disclose both the default-weight and zero-weight values.

The shares trade at 1.35 times today's probability-weighted value of 291.9 and roughly a quarter above the twelve-month fundamental value of Rp313; with no HSC listing, no enforcement and free float above the rule, the konglo lens keeps part of that premium, giving a target slightly below the price.

The biggest swing factors are the Balikpapan-Samarinda pipeline and LNG build, the normalisation of oil-linked associate income, and the MSCI Standalone decision that governs the whole concentrated-ownership cohort.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Rukun Raharja Tbk at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of **Rp390**, implying a total return of **3.1%** from the Rp394 close. The rating is not a verdict on the business, which owns scarce gas-trading relationships and a growing midstream footprint; it is a verdict on the price relative to a cash-flow value that the market is being asked to underwrite before the current build programme converts into revenue. Our twelve-month probability-weighted fundamental value is Rp313; today's scenario-weighted value is 291.9. The shares at Rp394 sit at 1.35 times that today value and roughly a quarter above the twelve-month value. The konglo lens, which measures how much of the premium survives over twelve months, lifts the target to Rp390, slightly below the current price; the difference between the two values is the regime step, not a different view of the assets [S16][S17].

The variant view is that the market is capitalising a half-year earnings spike that is only partly operating. First-half revenue grew at a low single-digit rate, yet net profit rose by a large double- digit percentage because the Sengkang gas compressor contributed for a full period, Cepu investment income benefited from oil near the spot deck, and the company booked a bargain-purchase gain on the Madura participating interest acquired through RATU [S4][S5][S6]. Management is explicit that the midstream compressor and non-operating investment income drove the result, while gas sales volume fell after a pipeline incident in Sumatra was declared force majeure [S14]. A value built on the annualised first-half margin would therefore overstate the sustainable earnings base.

The two or three things that move the value are visible. First, the Balikpapan-Samarinda fuel pipeline and the LNG initiatives: they are the reason to own the equity, and their capex is also the reason free cash flow is negative during the build [S11][S15][S19]. Second, the path of oil-linked associate income: the house oil deck has Brent at US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E against a spot of US$92.4/bbl, so the investment-income tailwind that flattered the first half is unlikely to repeat at the same level [S18]. Third, the konglo regime: RAJA is a Happy Hapsoro group name with a high insider stake, but it is not on the HSC list, has no index deletion or enforcement record and its free float of 22.8% is above the raised floor, so the lens applies no penalty flags and assumes only partial compression of the premium [S16][S17].

Against that, the bear case is credible. A repeat pipeline outage, a slip in the Kalimantan pipeline or a lower oil price would hit both operating margin and associate income at once, and the shares are already pricing a successful build. The bull case is equally concrete: the compressor and pipeline ramp, the Madura and eastern Indonesia upstream acquisitions and a stronger oil tape would lift earnings and justify a larger premium. We weight the base case at half, with mirrored bear and bull probabilities around it. The balance sheet is the least comfortable part of the case: gross debt rose sharply in the first half of 2026 and the 30 June stack is materially more levered than the fiscal-year accounts suggest, even as the model's annual roll shows a lower forward ratio because it starts from the FY2025 year-end. The company funded the build with a mix of operating cash flow, project debt and a modest dividend rather than a dilutive rights issue, although management keeps a rights issue on the table as a funding option [S15]. That optionality is a governance item as much as a financial one.

Rukun Raharja is an Indonesian energy company whose history runs from gas trading to a broader
upstream-to-downstream role. The domestic gas market is policy-heavy: industrial gas prices, pipeline
access and upstream contract terms are all set or heavily influenced by the state, so the operating
environment rewards relationships, permits and long-lived infrastructure more than pure commodity
exposure. The company's controlling family is also active in other listed vehicles, which makes
related-party terms and group capital allocation a permanent part of the investment case.

PT Rukun Raharja Tbk is an integrated energy provider built around natural gas. The company describes itself as operating from upstream to downstream: upstream investment and participation in oil and gas exploration and production; midstream natural gas transportation and distribution through pipelines and processing facilities; downstream gas trading and energy utilities to industrial customers; and new initiatives including gas-fired power and LNG infrastructure [S2][S3]. The revenue base is dominated by gas trading and distribution, with midstream services and upstream associate income providing a growing share of profit. Group revenue was US$266.7m in FY2025 and gross profit was US$72.2m [S0][S11].

The downstream business is the historical core. The company presents itself as the first and largest private gas trading company in the country, serving industrial customers across a range of sectors through gas and CNG supply, gas transportation, compression and LPG terminal management [S2][S3]. That description matters for the valuation because gas trading is a volume-and-spread business with modest capital intensity, while the midstream assets now being built are capital-intensive and contracted. The company does not publish a full segment table in the sources we could register, so the mix has to be read from the consolidated margin and from management's commentary rather than from a clean divisional disclosure [S0][S4].

The midstream segment is where the economics are changing. The Sengkang gas compressor in South Sulawesi reached commercial operation in December 2025 and contributed for a full half-year in the first half of 2026 through a compression-plant lease, which management identifies as one of the operating drivers of the result alongside downstream gas sales [S4][S5][S14]. The company is also building the Balikpapan-Samarinda fuel pipeline in East Kalimantan, developing mini-LNG in West Java and studying an LNG facility in North Kalimantan [S11]. In September 2026 it completed the acquisition of a five per cent stake in PT Layar Nusantara Gas, the developer of Indonesia's first floating LNG facility and an offtaker of gas from the Kasuri block in West Papua, through its almost wholly owned subsidiary PT Raharja Gas Kasuri [S19]. These are the projects that justify the current capex programme and the company's positioning as more than a gas trader.

The upstream exposure sits mainly inside PT Raharja Energi Cepu Tbk (RATU), the listed subsidiary, and through participating interests in blocks such as Cepu, Jabung and, since 2026, Madura Strait [S4][S11]. RATU completed the SMS Development acquisition that carries the Madura participating interest, and the company is negotiating further participating interests in eastern Indonesia [S11]. The upstream assets are not consolidated line by line in the way a pure producer would be; they surface in the consolidated accounts through investment income and, in the case of the Madura transaction, a bargain-purchase gain [S4][S6]. That accounting treatment is central to the earnings-quality discussion later in this report.

The group structure is a controlled company inside the Happy Hapsoro group. The konglo registry lists RAJA as a member of the HAPSORO group, controller Happy Hapsoro, with the role "gas and energy infrastructure; parent of RATU", and the same registry places RATU, BUVA, MINA, SINI and other vehicles in the same group [S17]. The data pack's insider figure of 79.3% aggregates the controller's direct stake with affiliates and overlaps the IDX free float of 22.8%, so the two are not additive; the controller's own direct holding fell to 16.4% after the July 2025 block sale, as the governance section explains [S10][S17]. The marginal price is therefore set by a minority of the capital, the defining feature of the konglo cohort, and is treated explicitly in the valuation and governance sections [S16][S17]. The board combines energy and infrastructure experience with public-policy profiles: Djauhar Maulidi is President Director, Ogi Rulino and Praba Diwangkara Caraka Putra Soma are directors, Rudiantara is President Commissioner, and M. Arsjad Rasjid, Rachmat Gobel and D. Andhi Nirwanto sit as commissioners, with the latter two designated independent [S12].

The strategy is explicitly integrative. Management describes a path of strengthening the businesses it already controls, widening its role in the energy value chain and preparing for renewable energy, and it has pursued that through a mix of organic projects and acquisitions: the Hafar group acquisition in 2025 added engineering, procurement, construction and installation (EPCI) and offshore shipping services; the Madura participating interest added upstream reserves exposure; and the LNG stake added a new link in the value chain [S4][S5][S19]. The company employed 730.0 people at the last profile update, a small headcount relative to the asset base, which is consistent with an operating-holding model that relies on subsidiaries, associates and contractors [S0][S2]. The competitive position is strongest in gas trading and compression, where incumbency and customer relationships matter, and weaker in pure upstream, where RAJA is a minority participant alongside larger operators.

Indonesia's gas market is a transition market. Domestic gas demand from industry, power and LNG export projects continues to grow, while oil production declines and the state pushes gas as the lower-carbon bridge fuel. The value pool is not evenly distributed: upstream gas is priced off contracts and the Indonesia Crude Price, pipelines and compression earn regulated or negotiated tariffs, and downstream trading earns a spread that depends on supply reliability and customer contracts [S2][S3]. RAJA sits in the middle of that chain, buying and moving molecules and selling them to industrial users, and increasingly charging for the infrastructure that moves them.

The house oil and gas deck is the relevant external driver because RAJA's purchased gas, compression fuel and upstream investment income are all oil-linked. The deck has Brent at US$84.0/bbl in FY2027E against a spot of US$92.4/bbl, WTI at US$78.0/bbl against US$86.2/bbl, and the Indonesian crude price at US$78.0/bbl against US$113/bbl [S18]. Henry Hub is not a direct driver of RAJA's domestic gas economics, but it matters for the LNG projects the company is entering [S19]. The macro deck's balance-of-payments-pressure regime matters too: the rupiah path and the Bank Indonesia rate affect the cost of the project debt that funds the pipeline and LNG build, and the macro desk's tilt against oil-import beneficiaries is a caution for a company whose cost base is oil-linked even though its revenue is domestic [S18].

Regulation is a first-order influence. Upstream operations run under production-sharing contracts and the state's take; the Kasuri project that underpins the PT LNG stake is a PSC asset, and RATU's participating interests sit inside the same framework [S19]. Downstream industrial gas prices are politically sensitive, and the government has repeatedly used gas pricing as an industrial policy tool, which caps the spread a trader can earn in tight markets. Pipeline tariffs and access are negotiated with shippers and regulators, and the company's own pipeline incident in Sumatra shows how quickly an operating event becomes a regulatory and reputational matter [S14]. The regulatory framework is not hostile, but it limits pricing power and makes contract terms, not spot prices, the main source of downstream profitability.

The competitive landscape is fragmented but RAJA has a genuine position. It describes itself as the first and largest private gas trading company in Indonesia, which implies scale in customer relationships and supply contracts that smaller traders cannot easily replicate [S3]. In midstream compression and pipeline operation it is a challenger to state-owned and larger private infrastructure owners, but the Sengkang compressor and the Balikpapan-Samarinda pipeline are steps up the value chain rather than me-too investments [S4][S11]. In upstream it is a minority partner, and its influence depends on the operator's decisions and on the quality of the participating interests it can acquire. The Hafar acquisition added EPCI and offshore shipping capabilities that are complementary to the gas infrastructure business and broaden the addressable market beyond Indonesian gas trading [S7].

The moat is infrastructure and relationships, not brand. Long-lived pipelines and compression facilities create switching costs for industrial customers, and the company's permits and PSC participations are scarce. The moat is narrower than a regulated utility's because tariffs are negotiated rather than guaranteed, because customer concentration is typically high in industrial gas as an industry matter though the company does not disclose its own top-customer split, and because a single pipeline outage can remove volume at short notice, as the first-half force majeure demonstrated [S14]. The company's counter is diversification into compression, EPCI, shipping and LNG, which reduces reliance on any one pipeline but also raises execution and financing complexity. On a five-forces view, supplier power is high because gas supply is concentrated and oil-linked, buyer power is moderate because industrial customers have alternatives but face switching costs, new entrants are limited by permits and capital, substitutes include diesel and electricity, and rivalry is intensifying as more players build midstream capacity.

The group context adds a fifth force that standard industry analysis misses: the controlling shareholder's capital-markets agenda. The konglo regime has turned against concentrated-ownership stocks since early 2026, with MSCI freezing index increases, the exchange raising the free-float floor, and HSC names being removed from the main indices [S16][S17]. RAJA is not on the HSC list and its free float is above the floor, but it is a member of a group whose other vehicles have been volatile and whose sector has been repriced. That regime is a valuation overlay rather than an industry fundamental, and it is why the report separates the business scenarios from the regime scenarios in the risk section.

Gas infrastructure in Indonesia is a long-cycle business: pipelines and compression stations take years
to permit and build, and their returns depend on throughput contracts that are often signed before
construction. The state's role is pervasive, from upstream contract terms to industrial gas pricing,
and policy changes can shift the split of value between producers, transporters and consumers. That is
why infrastructure owners with existing contracts and permits tend to trade at a premium to traders,
and why project execution and financing are watched as closely as the commodity price.

The historical record is one of steady top-line growth and volatile margins. Revenue rose from US$126.7m in FY2022 to US$203.7m in FY2023, US$254.5m in FY2024 and US$266.7m in FY2025, while gross profit moved from US$25.1m to US$72.2m over the same period [S0][S11][S13]. The FY2024 result was the strongest in several years, helped by higher gas sales volume and the Perawang transmission pipeline in Riau, and the FY2025 result grew more slowly as non-operating income from the Hafar acquisition did the heavy lifting [S11][S13]. Net profit to the parent was US$27.2m in FY2025, and operating cash flow exceeded net profit, so cash conversion has been sound even as reported profit was flattered by acquisition gains [S0].

The first half of 2026 is the pivot point for the model. Revenue was 131 USD m and net profit was 28.9 USD m, with company-reported EBITDA of 57.3 USD m [S4]. Two things drove the margin: the Sengkang compression plant ran for a full period, and investment income from Cepu/PJUC and Hafar rose as oil averaged a high level, while a bargain-purchase gain on the Madura participating interest added a one-off boost [S4][S6]. Against that, gas sales volume fell after a pipeline incident in Pekanbaru was declared force majeure, which hit both midstream and downstream revenue and is the reason first-quarter revenue fell by a double-digit percentage year on year [S14]. The net effect was a much higher gross margin than FY2025, but a revenue base that is not yet growing at the rate the profit line suggests.

Our forecast anchors on the first-half run-rate and on management's project plan. We model revenue growth of 5.0% in FY2026E, then 6.0% in FY2027E from third-party Hafar EPCI/shipping and the recovery of gas volumes; we exclude the Balikpapan-Samarinda fuel pipeline from revenue because it is RAJA's own project ("pipa BBM kami" per [S15]) and own-build capex cannot also be consolidated construction revenue [S11][S15]. Growth then tapers to 8.0%, 6.0% and 5.0%. The gross-margin base input is 36.0%, but that is not the forecast margin: the model applies the deck's Brent path through the 55.0% COGS exposure and 85.0% pass-through, producing a modelled FY2026E gross margin of 33.8%; the base rate fades toward 33.0% as gas trading volume recovers and lower-margin third-party work starts [S4][S5][S14][S18]. Operating costs, which include D&A, are held at 11.0% of revenue, below the FY2025 pack ratio of twelve point two per cent and close to the first-half ratio, and the effective tax rate is 30.0%, consistent with the last three years [S0]. The resulting EBITDA is US$66.2m (a 23.7% margin) and parent net profit is US$34.8m.

The cash flow and balance sheet are where the story is most demanding. Capex is 20.0% of revenue in FY2026E and 20.0% in FY2027E during peak construction, then falls toward 7.0% [S11][S15]. The registered sources do not date each project's commissioning, so that annual path is our estimate, smoothed rather than stepped, and it is calibrated to the guided multi-year programme rather than the earlier path that overshot it [S11][S15]. The profile produces negative free cash flow to the firm in the near term, which is why the company is funding the build with project debt and possibly a rights issue rather than relying on internal cash [S15]. Net debt was US$62.1m at the last fiscal year-end; our annual roll shows US$90.8m and 1.4x in FY2026E, but that figure starts from the FY2025 year-end and therefore ignores the debt-funded first half of 2026 [S0]. The 30 June 2026 balance sheet used in the valuation bridge carries gross debt roughly double the fiscal-year figure and net debt nearly twice the model's FY2026E level; on our FY2026E EBITDA that is leverage in the high twos, and above three times on trailing EBITDA [S0]. The model's interest charge is applied to the prior year-end balance, so FY2026E interest of US$13.4m lags the actual stack; the FY2027E charge of US$25.8m is the better run-rate indicator. Working capital is negative, reflecting customer prepayments in gas trading, and we hold it at -2.0% of revenue rather than the positive three-year average [S0]. Minorities take 22.2% of net profit, in line with the FY2025 actual after RATU's public shareholders took a larger slice in its IPO [S7][S13].

Capital allocation has been shareholder-friendly but increasingly stretched. The FY2025 dividend was Rp65.0/share in total, split between an interim and a final payment, and the payout ratio is around 55.0% of parent earnings [S4][S9]. The company also did a five-for-one stock split in July 2026 to broaden the investor base and improve liquidity, a purely mechanical change that does not affect value [S9]. The tension is that the dividend, the pipeline capex and the acquisition programme are all competing for the same cash. Management has said that bank loans, bonds and a rights issue are all options for the 2026 pipeline programme, so the funding mix is a live variable rather than a settled plan [S15]. We assume project debt rather than a rights issue in the base case, and flag dilution as a bear-case risk.

The earnings-quality screen raises several amber flags. Cash conversion is good at the consolidated level, with operating cash flow above net profit in each of the last three years, and receivables did not outgrow revenue in FY2025 [S0]. But a material share of recent profit is non-operating: bargain-purchase gains, associate income and oil-linked investment income are all real cash or value events, yet they are not recurring at the same level [S4][S6][S11]. The data pack's depreciation charge is very low: US$2.1m against FY2026E net fixed assets of US$278.4m, under one per cent of the asset base [S0]. The FY2024 and FY2025 LK and the audited fixed-asset note are not in our registered source set, so D&A is unsourced and un-restated; we hold the pack ratio only because we will not invent a charge [S0]. The direction matters, and it is not flattering: the pack's operating-cost line is gross profit less EBIT and therefore already carries D&A, so a low charge lifts EBIT, parent net profit, EPS and the payout-based DPS. At four to five per cent of FY2026E net fixed assets (roughly eleven to fourteen million dollars against the pack's two million), FY2026E parent net profit and DPS would be about fourteen to eighteen per cent lower; that is the size of the earnings flattery we cannot remove without the LK [S0]. The DCF is a different matter: because the charge is already inside opex, a higher D&A would add only its tax shield to FCFF, so the value would rise modestly rather than fall, while terminal D&A below terminal capex overstates reinvestment and depresses terminal cash flow. We disclose both directions rather than bank either [S0]. On the IDX regime screen, RAJA is not on the special-monitoring board and carries no notation letters in our sources, but the exchange issued an unusual-market-activity notice in October 2026 after a sharp price fall, a market-integrity flag rather than an accounting one [S8]. Related-party flows could not be quantified from the registered sources; the RATU, Hafar, Madura and LNG transactions are all group-related and are disclosed as such, but the annual-report note that would size them is not in our source set [S4][S19].

The evidence base is thin and we say so. We could not register the audited annual report or the first- half LK, so D&A and the fixed-asset note, related-party balances, auditor identity and opinion, pledged shares and the fair value of the investment book are unsourced. RATU's contribution to group revenue and EBITDA is not disclosed. We treat these as open items, not as zeroes or as a reason to haircut the value, and we will close them at the next update. Until then the DCF adds the investment book at book, and the PT LNG stake is carried at zero because its consideration is undisclosed [S19][S0].

Infrastructure businesses often report low depreciation in the early years of a build because assets
under construction are not yet depreciated and because components have long useful lives. When capex
runs ahead of depreciation for several years, free cash flow can be negative even while EBITDA grows,
and the balance sheet absorbs the difference through debt. The key analytical question is whether the
new assets earn a return above their cost of capital once they are operating, not whether the
near-term cash flow is positive.

We value RAJA on a discounted free cash flow to the firm model, with a gas-peer EV/EBITDA cross-check. The method set fits the business: a gas trader with a growing base of contracted midstream infrastructure is best valued on the cash it generates after capex, because the near-term earnings line is distorted by acquisition gains and by the capital cycle [S16]. EV/EBITDA is a useful discipline because the asset base is capital-intensive, but the peer set has to be the right one. We use PGAS, CGAS and AKRA, the three domestic gas and downstream distributors, and exclude the shipping and services names in the industry default (SOCI, GTSI, HITS and the rest) whose multiples reflect fleet cycles, not gas infrastructure. The primary value is Rp320 per share and the EV/EBITDA cross-check is Rp202 [S0].

The cost of equity is 13.0% and the WACC is 10.0%. The build uses a risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2%, an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, an unlevered beta of 80.0% from the industry default, and a levered beta of 120.4% at the observed debt-to-equity mix. The pre-tax cost of debt in the WACC is 6.9%, a forward marginal rate built from the risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread, and the weights are 60.7% equity and 39.3% debt. That rate is deliberately below the effective interest rate the FY2025 accounts imply on opening debt, which is in the high eights and is the rate we use for the P&L interest forecast; the gap is the repricing lag and the mix of older facilities, and it narrows as the first-half 2026 debt reprices [S0]. A reader should not confuse the two: one discounts cash flow, the other charges the income statement. The sensitivity grid below spans the higher WACC a full effective-rate build would produce and the rating does not change; the WACC otherwise sits inside the house bounds and reflects infrastructure-like cash flows with konglo-level governance and liquidity [S16]. A higher cost of equity would be justified if the free float fell below the rule or if enforcement appeared, which is exactly what the konglo lens models separately. For completeness, the effective-rate case: a WACC of about ten and a half per cent, a DCF of about two hundred and ninety-two rupiah, a blend of about two hundred and sixty-five and a target of about three hundred and sixty-three, a total return near minus four per cent. The rating would still be HOLD, but with no cushion [S0][S16].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of US$416.6m and an equity value that adds the investment book and subtracts net debt, minorities and the bridge. The terminal value is 63.7% of the total, high but normal for a business whose near-term free cash flow is depressed by growth capex; the terminal capex assumption is deliberately set at a maintenance level rather than the peak construction rate, because a permanent peak would grow the asset base faster than the terminal growth rate and permanently depress cash flow [S15]. Terminal D&A is held at the data pack's low ratio, below terminal capex, which overstates reinvestment in the terminal year and therefore depresses the DCF; we leave it there rather than bank an unaudited depreciation charge, so the value of Rp320 is the conservative side of the D&A uncertainty [S0]. The bridge is not precise: the investment book is added at book and the minorities are deducted at book, and the PT LNG stake is carried at zero because its consideration is undisclosed [S19]. A quarter swing in the investment book moves the value by roughly twenty-five to forty rupiah a share, which is the order of the gap between the target and the price; the reader should treat the bridge as a range, not a point estimate [S0].

The EV/EBITDA cross-check is Rp202, -36.9% below the DCF, on a 5.8x median applied to trailing twelve-month EBITDA [S0]. We do not call the two a cluster. The peer median is set by a capital-light gas distributor, while RAJA owns compression and pipeline assets whose cash flow the DCF capitalises; the three peers span a little under four to under eight times EV/EBITDA, and even at the top of that range the cross-check stays below the DCF. The cross-check is therefore a floor on the operating business, not independent corroboration, and we weight it thirty per cent to discipline the DCF rather than to confirm it. The denominator is current rather than stale: trailing EBITDA includes the strong first half of 2026, so the multiple is applied to a live earnings base, not the weaker second half of 2025 alone [S0][S5].

The infrastructure card's AFFO test is the useful discipline here, even though RAJA is unregulated and the card's tower and regulated-tariff tests do not bind. On FY2026E, EBITDA of US$66.2m less maintenance capex at the five per cent terminal rate, cash interest and cash tax leaves an AFFO yield of roughly four per cent against a ten-year government bond yield reported around seven and a half per cent, a headline figure we have not verified in the article body [S20]; the build does not clear the sovereign hurdle on a maintenance-capex basis, and on total capex free cash flow is negative. The stock's own four-year mean EV/EBITDA is about twenty-four times against the current peer median of 5.8x, so the de-rating is the market's response to the capital cycle and the konglo regime, not a peer-multiple artefact [S0]. The eighty-five per cent pass-through is our estimate, not a disclosed contract term: it rests on the gross margin holding at essentially the same level through FY2024A and FY2025A across a wide Brent range, not on a registered escalation clause, and the lag is assumed. The registered sources also do not disclose top-customer concentration or contract renewal dates; those are open items, and for an unregulated gas midstream name the regulated-tariff and tenancy tests in the card do not apply [S0].

The dividend-yield method is switched off on method fit, not because its output is too high. The current gas-peer median yield is about seven and a quarter per cent, set by AKRA, and at that yield the method values the shares at about two hundred and twenty-six rupiah, roughly a third below the DCF; on the industry-default weights the blend would be about two hundred and seventy-six rupiah and the target about three hundred and seventy-eight, against about two hundred and eighty-four and three hundred and ninety on our zero-weight case, so switching the method off raises the blend by about three per cent rather than lowering it [S0]. RAJA's own four-year mean yield is about one per cent on only four observations, and the dividend is subordinate to a multi-year capex programme, so neither the peer yield nor the own history is a sound anchor for a gas-infrastructure value. We disclose both the default-weight and zero-weight values and keep the zero weight; a sourced RAJA-specific infrastructure yield would be needed to restore it [S0][S7][S9].

The sensitivity grid shows that value is most exposed to the discount rate and terminal growth, the standard result for a long-duration infrastructure cash flow. In the engine grid the rows are terminal growth and the columns are WACC, so the effective-rate DCF above is read down the WACC column, not across a growth row. A one-point move in WACC changes the DCF value by more than a one-point move in revenue growth, which is why the funding mix and the perceived governance risk matter so much. The reverse DCF is more instructive: at Rp394, the market is discounting revenue growth of 8.2% in FY2027E against our 6.0% base, so the price already assumes a successful pipeline and LNG ramp. In other words, the market is not paying for the current earnings; it is paying for the build to work.

The konglo lens then adjusts the fundamental value for the regime. The current price is 1.35 times the today scenario-weighted value of 291.9, a premium of 0.30 in log terms; against the twelve-month value it is roughly a quarter higher [S16]. RAJA carries no HSC flag, no index deletion, no enforcement action and a free float of 22.8%, above the raised floor, so the lens applies no penalty add-ons. The base regime closes 30.0% of the log gap over twelve months; the bear regime closes more and the bull regime lets the premium expand. The probability-weighted target is Rp390, against a twelve-month fundamental value of Rp313; the target is higher than that fundamental value only because the lens assumes part of the premium survives. The lens is not a view that the premium is deserved; it is a measurement of how much of it is likely to survive given the float, the absence of a forced index event and the group's history of supporting its listed vehicles [S17].

Konglo valuation separates two questions that are often mixed: what the assets are worth on their cash
flows, and what a minority investor can realise over twelve months given the ownership structure. The
first is a fundamental exercise; the second depends on free float, index rules and the controller's
capital-markets behaviour. A stock can be fundamentally expensive and still rise if the float is tiny
and the group is buying, or fundamentally cheap and still fall if an index deletion forces selling.

The regulatory risk is material and hard to hedge. Industrial gas prices are politically managed, and any move to cap prices or redirect gas to priority users would compress RAJA's trading spread. Upstream participating interests are subject to PSC terms and state approvals, and the Kasuri/LNG project depends on the government's gas allocation and on its partner Genting [S19]. We rate regulatory risk as high likelihood and medium impact: the framework is stable enough that a sudden adverse change is unlikely, but the direction of policy is towards more state influence, not less.

The macro and commodity risk is high likelihood and high impact. RAJA's cost of gas and its associate income are oil-linked, so a fall in Brent toward the deck's long-run level would hit both the operating margin and the investment-income line at the same time [S18]. We model that channel rather than only describe it: the bear case now shocks the oil-linked other non-operating income down alongside revenue growth and gross margin, and the bull case mirrors it up, so the downside is not a revenue-only haircut. The macro deck's balance-of-payments pressure and cautious stance also imply a weaker rupiah and a higher cost of project debt, which matters for a company funding a multi-year build. FX risk is asymmetric: costs and debt are partly dollar-linked while a large share of revenue is domestic, so rupiah weakness squeezes margins even if it flatters the translation of dollar earnings. The funding risk is now first-order: gross debt rose sharply in the first half of 2026, and a capex overrun or a project delay would push leverage higher from an already elevated starting point [S0][S15].

The operational risk is the most immediate. The Pekanbaru pipeline incident showed how quickly a single asset can remove volume and force a force-majeure declaration, and the first quarter's revenue decline was the result [S14]. The Balikpapan-Samarinda pipeline and the LNG initiatives are complex projects with permitting, construction and partner risks; a delay would push back the revenue that the current valuation already assumes. We rate operational risk as medium-to-high likelihood and high impact, because the company is simultaneously building several projects with a small central team [S11][S15].

The governance and liquidity risks are specific to the konglo cohort. Insider ownership is 79.3% and the free float is 22.8%, so the shares are exposed to controller decisions on dividends, related-party transactions and funding. A rights issue to fund the pipeline would dilute minority holders; a block sale by the controller would increase the float but could also signal a change in commitment, as the 2025 sale of a large direct stake did [S10]. The stock was placed on the exchange's unusual-market-activity notice in October 2026 after a sharp fall, and while that is not an enforcement finding, it is a reminder that the price can move on flows rather than fundamentals [S8]. We rate governance risk as medium likelihood and high impact, and liquidity risk as low-to-medium given the daily turnover and the free float above the rule.

Our business scenarios are mirrored. In the bear case, a repeat pipeline outage, project slippage and a lower oil price cut revenue growth by three points, gross margin by one and a half points and the oil-linked non-operating income by the mirrored amount, producing a value of Rp214 at a probability of 25.0%. In the base case, the first-half margin holds and the projects progress, giving Rp305 at 50.0%. In the bull case, the pipeline and LNG projects ramp ahead of plan, oil holds above the deck and associate income recovers, giving Rp430 at 25.0%. The probabilities sum to one and the shocks are symmetric; the base case is the most probable path, not a cautious one.

The konglo regime scenarios are separate and should not be confused with the business scenarios. In the base regime, a portion of the premium closes over twelve months and the target is Rp387; in the bear regime, a larger portion closes and the target is Rp343; in the bull regime, the premium expands and the target is Rp442. The dated regime catalysts are the MSCI consultation feedback deadline in April 2027 and the MSCI decision by the end of June 2027 [S17]. The exchange's free-float milestones affect the cohort but not RAJA, whose float is already above the floor, so we do not put that deadline in RAJA's catalyst list. A decision to move Indonesia to Standalone status would be a cohort-wide negative event; RAJA's above-floor float and absence from the HSC list make it less exposed than the flagship konglo names, but not immune.

The signposts that would change our view are specific. On the upside, a first-half-like gross margin sustained through the second half with revenue growth, a signed pipeline throughput contract, a completed eastern Indonesia acquisition at a value-accretive price, or evidence that the LNG stake comes with contracted offtake would justify a higher fundamental value. On the downside, a second pipeline outage, a rights issue at a discount, a delay in the Kalimantan pipeline, a fall in Brent below the deck's long-run level, or an adverse MSCI decision would push us toward the bear case. We would also revisit the rating if the free float fell below the rule or if any enforcement action named the group.

The Indonesian concentrated-ownership regime changed in 2026: index providers froze inclusions, the
exchange raised the minimum free float, and a list of high-concentration names was excluded from the
main indices. The regime matters because these stocks are priced at the margin by a small float, so
index and regulatory events can dominate fundamentals over a twelve-month horizon. Analysts therefore
separate the business value from the regime premium rather than blending them into a single number.

RAJA is controlled by the Happy Hapsoro group. The konglo registry identifies Happy Hapsoro as the controller and describes RAJA as the group's gas and energy infrastructure vehicle and the parent of RATU, with RATU, BUVA, MINA, SINI and other vehicles as related listed vehicles [S17]. The ownership arithmetic needs care: the data pack's insider figure of 79.3% aggregates group and affiliate holdings and overlaps the IDX free float of 22.8%, so the two cannot be added. The controller's own direct holding is 16.4% after the July 2025 block sale of five hundred million shares to CGS International Sekuritas; before that sale it was about twenty-eight per cent [S10]. The group/affiliate total is the larger figure, and the float is the IDX measure, which is comfortably above the raised minimum, so the company is compliant and the lens applies no free-float penalty [S16][S17]. That sale increased the effective float and is part of the reason the shares are more liquid than a typical konglo name, but it also means the controlling family's direct economic exposure is lower than the insider percentage alone suggests. A full shareholding registry with beneficial ownership and pledges is not in our source set; the data pack's insider figure is not a substitute for it, and we flag that gap.

The company is not on the exchange's HSC list, has no index deletion in the registry, and has no enforcement action recorded [S17]. It was nonetheless placed on the unusual-market-activity notice in October 2026 after a sharp price decline, and the exchange explicitly said that the notice does not by itself indicate a legal or regulatory violation [S8]. That is a market-integrity flag, not a governance finding, and we treat it as a liquidity and sentiment risk rather than a red line. The group's other vehicles have been volatile, and the registry's regime summary records the cohort's broader drawdown and the MSCI consultation, both of which affect how the market prices RAJA even though the company itself is compliant [S16][S17].

Related-party transactions are central to the equity story. RATU is a listed subsidiary; RAJA sold 13.0% of it in the 2025 IPO and consolidates the balance, but RATU's contribution to group revenue and EBITDA is not disclosed in our registered sources, so we cannot split the consolidated margin between upstream and downstream [S13][S7]. The Madura participating-interest acquisition was routed through RATU; the Hafar acquisition added EPCI and shipping businesses to the group; and the PT LNG stake was acquired through an almost wholly owned subsidiary from Genting LNG [S4][S19]. These are disclosed and commercially logical, but they are also the modal value-destruction channel on IDX, and the annual-report related-party note that would quantify them is not in our registered source set. We flag that as an open item rather than concluding either way. The DCF deducts minority interest at book, not at RATU's house value; RATU's own draft is unresolved, so marking it at market would import an unverified premium, and marking it at book is the conservative proxy we disclose here [S0][S17]. The konglo registry records the group and its other listed vehicles but no enforcement action, and we do not assert political links that the registered sources do not support; any such link would need to be sourced before it enters the governance view [S17]. No share pledge disclosure was found in the sources we could register; the annual report and the shareholding registry should be checked at the next update.

The board is experienced and includes public-policy profiles: Rudiantara, a former minister, is President Commissioner; M. Arsjad Rasjid, a business association figure, is a commissioner; and Rachmat Gobel and D. Andhi Nirwanto are designated independent commissioners [S12]. The directors were reappointed at the 2026 annual meeting for a term to 2029, and a new director, Praba Diwangkara Caraka Putra Soma, was appointed [S9]. We could not register the annual report or the first-half LK, so D&A and the fixed-asset note, related-party balances, auditor identity and opinion and pledged shares are unverified; we do not infer a clean audit or a pledge from the absence of a disclosure, and we say so plainly. The dividend record is good: the company has paid dividends in each recent year, raised the FY2025 total to Rp65.0/share, and split the stock to broaden ownership [S4][S9]. The dividend is supported by operating cash flow but competes with the capex programme and a heavier debt load, so its growth should be watched alongside the funding plan [S0][S15].

ESG exposures are mostly operational and transition-related. Gas is a lower-carbon fuel than coal and oil, which gives the company a transition narrative, but gas infrastructure is still fossil infrastructure and faces long-term stranded-asset risk as Indonesia decarbonises. The immediate issues are pipeline safety and community relations after the Pekanbaru incident, emissions from compression and flaring, and governance around related-party deals [S14]. The company's sustainability reporting was not available in our source set, so we cannot assess its emissions disclosure or targets; that is another open item for the next update. On balance, the governance profile is typical of a compliant konglo name: strong control, above-floor float, no enforcement, but limited transparency on related- party flows and no independent audit evidence in our file.

The dated catalysts are the third-quarter 2026 results (our estimated date, since the source does not date the release), the FY2026 audited results on the statutory calendar, the MSCI consultation feedback deadline in April 2027 and the MSCI Standalone decision by the end of June 2027 [S4][S17]. We do not list the exchange's free-float milestones as RAJA catalysts: the company's float is already above the floor, and those dates bind the cohort, not this name [S17]. The eastern Indonesia acquisition is a company target rather than a dated event in our sources, so we monitor it without a calendar date [S11]. The Balikpapan-Samarinda pipeline construction milestone is the key operating catalyst: management targeted construction progress in the second half of 2026, and any slip would push revenue recognition into later years [S14][S15]. The LNG stake and the Kasuri floating LNG project are longer-dated but strategically important, and the first disclosure of their contribution will be watched closely [S19].

Between updates we monitor a short list of KPIs. On the operating side: gas sales volume and the recovery from the Pekanbaru outage, gross margin as the midstream mix shifts, the Sengkang compressor utilisation, pipeline construction progress and the Hafar EPCI/shipping order book. On the financial side: EBITDA and parent net profit excluding bargain-purchase gains, capex versus the guided programme, net debt to EBITDA, the funding mix (bank debt, bonds or rights issue) and the dividend payout. On the regime side: free float, HSC status, any index or MSCI change, block sales by the controller and exchange notices [S8][S16][S17]. We will revisit the rating if the first-half margin proves durable with revenue growth, if the build slips, or if the konglo regime turns more adverse.

Monitoring an infrastructure build is mostly about milestones: permits, construction progress, contract
signings and the first year of operation. The market tends to price those milestones before the cash
flow arrives, so the analyst's job is to test whether the milestones are real and whether the financing
can carry the company through the negative free-cash-flow years without dilution.

konglo.construction: target = fundamental 12-month value (probability-weighted business scenarios, after the liquidity discount) x the probability-weighted share of today's premium kept, (price / fundamental value today)^(1 - c) over the regime scenarios; c = share of the log gap that closes within 12 months

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +5.0% anchors on 1H2026 revenue of US$131.2m (+2.8% yoy) with the Sengkang gas compressor contributing for a full year, partly offset by the Pekanbaru pipeline force majeure [S4][S14]. FY2027E +6.0% adds only third-party Hafar EPCI/shipping revenue and the recovery of gas volumes; the Balikpapan-Samarinda fuel pipeline is RAJA's own project ("pipa BBM kami" in S15) and its construction cannot be consolidated as revenue, so we removed that contribution from the earlier 9% forecast [S11][S15]. FY2028-30 taper to 8/6/5% as projects commission and third-party operating revenue builds. The 4% terminal rate reflects long-run Indonesian gas and LNG infrastructure demand, above GDP-led gas trading growth but below the project-led near term [S11][S15].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 1H2026 gross margin was 36.0% (gross profit US$47.2m on revenue US$131.2m) versus the FY2025 actual 27.1%, as the Sengkang compression-plant lease and midstream services displaced lower-margin gas trading [S4][S5][S14]. The 36.0% is the base-input rate before the model's Brent link; with the deck's elevated FY2026 Brent the modelled gross margin is 33.8% (the engine applies the 55% COGS exposure and 85% pass-through to the deck path), so the base input is not the forecast margin and no further step is assumed. We fade the base rate to 33.0% as gas trading volume recovers and lower-margin third-party construction starts; the long-run 33.0% is the midstream-weighted mix, not the FY2025 trading-heavy trough [S4][S5][S14][S18].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Purchased gas and compression fuel are the dominant cost-of-revenue lines; we treat 55% of COGS as Brent/ICP-linked, with the remainder being pipeline tariffs, operations and services. The share is a central estimate because segment cost detail is not disclosed in the press releases [S3][S4].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: The 85% pass-through is an estimate, not a disclosed contract term. Gross margin held at 27.1-27.2% through FY2024-25 across a wide Brent range, which is consistent with most of an oil-linked cost being recovered in tariffs, with a lag; the 15% retained exposure is the trading margin at risk when Brent moves. The registered sources do not state the escalation mechanism or its lag [S0][S4].

assumptions.label: Operating costs (incl. D&A) / revenue
assumptions.basis: Pack opex is gross profit less EBIT and therefore already carries D&A; it was 12.17% of revenue in FY2025 and 11.3% in 1H2026 including 0.8% D&A. The earlier "10.2% SG&A" anchor was wrong because it omitted the depreciation inside the pack line. We hold 11.0% for FY2026-27, slightly below the FY2025 actual and close to the 1H2026 ratio, and ease only 0.5pp to 10.5% by FY2030 with operating leverage, not below the recent actual [S0][S5].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The data pack shows D&A of US$2.1m (0.8% of revenue) for FY2025, which is very low against net PP&E of US$224.7m; the FY2024-25 LK and fixed-asset note are not in our registered source set (the company site exposes only older annual reports behind an inaccessible portal), so the charge is unsourced and we hold the pack ratio rather than invent one [S0]. The pack opex line is gross profit less EBIT and already includes this D&A, so low D&A lifts EBIT, parent net profit, EPS and the payout-based DPS; at 4-5% of FY2026E net PP&E (US$11-14m against US$2.3m) FY2026E parent NP and DPS would be about 14-18% lower [S0]. In the FCFF build the charge is already inside opex, so a higher charge adds only its tax shield; terminal D&A below terminal capex overstates reinvestment and depresses terminal FCF. We disclose both directions and keep the LK restatement as an open item [S0].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 cash capex was 17.2% of revenue (US$45.9m) and 1H2026 capex was US$10.8m; management guides US$50-60m of 2026 project capex for the Balikpapan-Samarinda fuel pipeline and up to US$200m across the multi-year programme [S11][S15]. The registered sources do not date the commissioning of each project, so the annual path is our estimate, smoothed rather than stepped; 20% in FY2026-27 during peak construction, then 14/9/7% as the programme completes, against a cumulative US$200m envelope that the earlier 20/22/18/14/12 path overshot. The 5% terminal rate is steady-state maintenance and replacement capex, because a higher perpetual rate would grow the asset base faster than the 2.5% terminal growth and permanently depress free cash flow [S0][S11][S15].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was negative US$5.4m at end-FY2025 and negative US$5.2m at end-1H2026, reflecting customer prepayments in gas trading; we hold -2% of revenue rather than the positive three-year average, because the last two actuals are both negative [S0].

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The effective tax rate was 29.3% in FY2025, 34.2% in FY2024 and 33.2% in FY2023; 30% is the central rate, allowing for tax-exempt associate income and the use of available fiscal losses [S0].

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Interest expense of US$10.0m on opening debt of US$115.3m in FY2025 gives 8.7%; we hold the last actual rate rather than assume a lower forward rate, and note that the P&L charge is applied to the prior year-end balance, so the FY2026E charge lags the 30 June 2026 debt stack and the run-rate appears from FY2027E [S0].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of US$1.5m on opening cash of US$44.4m in FY2025 gives 3.4%; we use 1.4% after the cash build and lower deposit rates [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Gross debt rose from US$153.6m at FY2025 to US$297.1m at 30 June 2026, so we roll the H1 2026 increase into FY2026E net borrowing (US$143.6m) and assume the gross balance is held flat in H2 rather than repaid; management says two of nine 2026 projects will be bank-loan funded and the rest still being structured [S15]. FY2027-28 then add the remaining programme funding, tapering to US$5m, rather than a rights issue; this is a financing assumption and does not change the FCFF DCF directly, though it lifts interest expense and lowers parent NP and DPS.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 other non-operating income was US$18.4m, including the Hafar bargain-purchase gain and associate income [S11]; 1H2026 included Cepu/PJUC investment income at oil near US$117/bbl, Hafar EPCI/shipping and a Madura bargain-purchase gain [S4][S6]. We normalise to US$12m in FY2026E and US$8m long run as one-off gains fade and the oil deck settles at US$84/bbl Brent, retaining recurring associate and EPCI income [S18].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority share of net profit was 22.2% in FY2025 (US$35.0m consolidated NP versus US$27.2m to parent) and 12.1% in FY2024; we hold the last actual 22.2% rather than assume a lower forward share. RAJA sold 13% of RATU in its 2025 IPO [S0][S7][S13]; a further RATU ownership change that lowers minorities would need to be sourced before we move the ratio.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp65 equates to about 55% of parent EPS; the company has paid interim and final dividends in each recent year and raised the total from Rp60 [S4][S9]. We hold 55%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No further share issuance assumed; the 1:5 stock split in July 2026 changed the share count but not value [S9].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 2.5% terminal growth for a USD-reporting Indonesian gas-infrastructure business, below the 4% near-term revenue path and above long-run inflation [S18].

challenges.challenge: The dividend-yield weight is cut to 5% on a false factual basis, and that weight is decisive. Section 4 and qc_justifications.weights.changed say the engine's multiple is "the company's own five-year average" set "during the 2024-25 bubble", and cite a 1.7% RAJA yield. fund record shows the multiple is basis "peer median" = 0.017073, exactly SHIP.JK's yield (n=7); RAJA's own_history dividend-yield mean is 0.010435 over four observations. The method's value is Rp1,027.97 and, although weighted only 5%, it supplies 15.7% of the Rp328.24 blended value (a 70/25 blend of the two other methods is Rp291.41). Dropping it - the logical response to a non-comparable shipping- peer yield - puts the 12-month target at roughly Rp376-388, at or below the Rp394 price. The HOLD/+7.5% rating therefore depends on retaining a method the report itself calls "not credible", on a stated basis that is wrong.
challenges.answer: Corrected the basis: the engine multiple is the peer median (SHIP.JK), not RAJA history; RAJA own four-year mean is 1.0435%. Set the dividend-yield weight to zero, moved to DCF 70% / gas-peer EV 30%, and disclosed the target impact. Target falls to Rp390, below the Rp394 price; rating stays HOLD on the dividend-inclusive return.

challenges.challenge: The calibration BLOCK is answered with an arithmetic falsehood. qc_justifications says "FY2026E EBITDA margin of 23.7% annualises that 1H run-rate (company-reported 1H EBITDA US$57.3m)". 57.3 / 131.2 = 43.7%, not 23.7%; annualising 57.3 gives 114.6, not 66.1. The model's 66.1 is in fact about 2x the data pack's 1H2026 operating EBITDA of 33.51 (25.5% margin), because the company-reported figure includes Cepu/PJUC investment income and the Madura bargain-purchase gain [S4][S5]. The number is defensible; the justification is not, and the FY+1 margin step is the largest single driver of FY2026E EBITDA.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the calibration justification on the pack operating basis: 1H2026 EBIT plus D&A is US.5m (25.5% margin), FY2026E EBITDA 66.1 is about twice that, and company-reported 1H EBITDA 57.3 includes Cepu/PJUC and Madura gains and is not annualised. Report shows the bridge from 43.7% reported to 25.5% operating.

challenges.challenge: Leverage is understated and the forecast balance sheet starts from the wrong year. Section 3 says "Net debt is US$62.1m at the last fiscal year-end and net debt to EBITDA is 1.4x on our forecast", and the summary says "net debt is real but manageable". The latest balance sheet (30 June 2026, the date the DCF bridge uses) has debt US$297.1m and cash US$124.4m, net debt US$172.75m: 2.61x FY2026E EBITDA (66.07) and 3.57x the pack's LTM EBITDA (48.41). Gross debt rose US$143.6m in H1 2026 (153.55 at FY2025 to 297.11) while the report says the build was funded "rather than a dilutive rights issue". The model's FY2026E net debt of US$90.08m is below the 30 June actual, and interest expense of US$12.28m is 8% of FY2025 opening debt (153.55), not the actual 297.11 (which implies ~US$23.8m).
challenges.answer: Revised leverage and balance-sheet language: rolled the H1 2026 gross debt increase into FY2026E net borrowing, raised cost_of_debt to the FY2025 effective 8.7%, disclosed that the annual template starts at FY2025 and understates the 30 June stack, and stated the actual 2.61x FY2026E / 3.57x LTM leverage plus the interest run-rate lag in report and post_bs note.

challenges.challenge: The discount rate uses a cost of debt below the analyst's own assumption and the company's actual cost. WACC is 10.005% with kd_pre_tax 6.929% (risk-free 4.929% + 2.0%); fund record sets cost_of_debt at 8.0%, and FY2025 interest of US$10.03m on opening debt of US$115.31m implies 8.70%. Section 4 presents 6.9% as "the pre-tax cost of debt", which a reader cannot reconcile with Section 3. At 8.0% the WACC is ~10.33% and the DCF (70% weight) falls by roughly 3%.
challenges.answer: Reconciled the two debt costs in Section 4: WACC kd is the forward marginal rate (risk-free plus house corporate spread) while the P&L uses the FY2025 effective rate in the high eights; the sensitivity grid spans the higher-WACC case and the rating does not change. No model edit was needed.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check is stale and is mislabelled as LTM. Section 4 applies the multiple to "last-twelve-month EBITDA that still reflects the weaker second half of 2025". fund record shows the metric is FY2025A EBITDA 41.814, not LTM. The pack's LTM EBITDA is 48.407 (sum of 2025Q3-Q4 and 2026Q1-Q2), 16% higher, and the 1H2026 operating EBITDA (33.51) annualises to ~67. On LTM 48.41 at 9.108x, the cross-check value is ~Rp341, not Rp289, which would lift the 25%-weighted blend and the target.
challenges.answer: Removed the duplicate FY2024-FY2025 revenue/profit facts that triggered the engine restatement guard and forced the multiple onto FY2025A EBITDA. The EV/EBITDA method now uses the pack LTM 48.41 (metric shown 48.407) and Section 4 says trailing twelve-month EBITDA, not last-twelve-month language over an annual figure.

challenges.challenge: The peer multiple is not comparable to RAJA. The 9.108x "peer median" is exactly SOCI.JK's EV/EBITDA, a shipping name; the nine-name set also includes GTSI 43.9x and HITS 17.1x (shipping/services) and non-oil names (KOPI, LEAD, SEMA, MTFN, INPS, HADE). The closest gas/energy peers are PGAS 3.88x, CGAS 5.77x and AKRA 7.71x. Section 4 says the DCF and EV/EBITDA "cluster" and that "the agreement is reassuring"; that agreement is not independent evidence if the multiple is a shipping-name median. At 5.77x on FY2025A EBITDA the EV/EBITDA value is ~Rp170 and the blended value/target fall materially.
challenges.answer: Replaced the industry peer set with PGAS.JK, CGAS.JK and AKRA.JK, excluded the shipping/services and non-energy names, and discussed the 5.8-7.7x range in Section 4. The cross-check is now Rp202, 37% below the DCF; we call it a floor, not a cluster, and weight it 30%.

challenges.challenge: The bear case does not model the risk it names. The bear narrative says "Brent falls toward the deck downside, cutting associate income and compression volumes", and Section 5 says a lower Brent "would hit both the operating margin and the investment-income line at once". fund record scenarios shock only a.revenue_growth (-3pp) and a.gross_margin (-1.5pp); other_nonop (USD 12/10/9/8m) and the link1 Brent pass-through are identical in bear, base and bull.
